title: Phantom Success, Silent Failure: Auditing the Success Checkers of Simulated Manipulation Benchmarks
trick: Have an LLM read a benchmark's task instruction and its success-checker code separately, stage the states where the two disagree in the unmodified simulator, and re-score released policies' rollouts with the repaired checker.
framing_stripped: Called 'SimAudit, an LLM-based pipeline that audits success checkers against task instructions' with two named error types, 'phantom success' (the checker accepts an execution that does not fulfil the instruction) and 'silent failure' (it rejects one that does); it is a four-stage test generator for hand-written reward functions (read instruction and code separately, guess up to four disagreement states with the checker's predicted verdict, write a probe that builds the state under physics in the benchmark's own simulator and reads the checker, have a VLM that never sees the code label rendered frames), followed by a hand-written second checker ('Verified': measure physical state instead of commanded values, add missing and remove unstated conditions, require the conditions to hold for one second) and a differential re-scoring of the same rollouts of released policies under both checkers (Table 2); the headline is 61 defects in 49 of 142 tasks across RoboTwin 2.0, RoboCasa365 and RoboDojo (40 phantom, 21 silent; Table 1) and a per-policy success-rate shift between -3.9 and +9.1 percentage points with rankings unchanged (sec. 4.4).
method_equations: The paper contains no equations; the following formalises its sec. 3.1 and Table 2 prose. A task has an instruction and a checker $c : \mathcal{S} \to \{0, 1\}$ on simulator states $s \in \mathcal{S}$. An episode $(s_0, \dots, s_T)$ with time limit $T$ is recorded as a success when $t^\ast = \min\{t \le T : c(s_t) = 1\}$ exists, and the episode ends at $t^\ast$ ('The benchmark ends the episode at the first state on which the checker returns success and records a success', sec. 3.1). Let $g(s) \in \{0, 1\}$ be the judgement of 'A person who reads the instruction and looks at the scene' (sec. 3.1) on the state at which the benchmark gives its verdict. A phantom success is $c(s_{t^\ast}) = 1$ with $g(s_{t^\ast}) = 0$; a silent failure is an episode with $c(s_t) = 0$ for all $t \le T$ while $g(s_T) = 1$ ('Both are judged on the state at which the benchmark gives its verdict; what the robot would have done after the episode ends does not count', sec. 3.1). A defect is counted only on a reachable state (produced by robot or scripted-expert motion under physics, or a settled pose after release); teleport-only states are 'not counted' (sec. 3.1); one defect per flaw per task. Audit pipeline (sec. 3.2): per task, the agent writes $\le 4$ hypotheses, each a state, the predicted $c$, the opposite $g$ and the responsible code line; a probe builds the state and the harness records $c$ and the first step at which it is true; 'agent-confirmed' means the probe returned the predicted $c$; a reviewer VLM that sees instruction, frames and $c$ per frame but 'never the code' labels valid / unrealistic / wrong / not shown, and only valid is counted. Funnel (sec. 1, App. D): 142 tasks, 568 proposed states, 183 agent-confirmed, 61 defects; on RoboTwin 2.0 the 91 agent-confirmed hypotheses split into 31 defects, 1 repeat, 37 unrealistic, 19 wrong, 3 not shown. Cost: '$0.78 in LLM calls and takes 18 minutes on average over the 142 tasks' (App. D). RoboTwin gripper proxy (App. C): with commanded gripper value $u_g$, the released checkers treat the gripper as open when $u_g > 0.8$ and as grasping when $u_g < 0.2$, read from the command rather than finger state. Verified checker $c'$ (sec. 3.3): measure physical state (a gripper 'holds an object when its links exert force on it'), add missing and remove unstated conditions, and require persistence, $c'_{\mathrm{ep}} = 1$ iff there is a $t$ with $c'(s_\tau) = 1$ for all $\tau \in [t, t + 1\,\mathrm{s}]$; thresholds 'stay as released unless a defect concerns the threshold itself'; validated on 1,233 expert episodes (all accepted) and the 61 defect states as a regression suite; $c'$ runs as an observer next to $c$ and never changes the state. Re-scoring (sec. 4.4, Table 2), per policy over $N$ episodes with the rollout continued past $t^\ast$: $$\Delta = \mathrm{SR}_{c'} - \mathrm{SR}_{c}, \quad \mathrm{Phan} = \frac{|\{e : c_e = 1, c'_e = 0\}|}{|\{e : c_e = 1\}|}, \quad \mathrm{Silent} = \frac{|\{e : c_e = 0, c'_e = 1\}|}{|\{e : c_e = 0\}|}, \quad \mathrm{Flip} = \frac{|\{e : c_e \neq c'_e\}|}{N},$$ where $\mathrm{SR}$ is the success rate in percent, $\Delta$ in percentage points, $c_e$ and $c'_e$ the episode verdicts of the original and Verified checkers. Table 2 (Orig. $\to$ Verif., $\Delta$; Phan; Silent; Flip, all in %): RoboTwin 2.0 (all 50 clean-setting tasks, official seeds and expert filter, App. E): LingBot-VA $93.1 \to 90.0$, $-3.1$; 3.3; 0.0; 3.1. LingBot-VLA 2.0 $93.9 \to 90.8$, $-3.1$; 3.4; 1.5; 3.3. Evo-1 $68.3 \to 65.5$, $-2.7$; 5.8; 3.9; 5.2. X-VLA $64.9 \to 61.6$, $-3.4$; 6.2; 2.0; 4.7. $\pi_{0.5}$ $46.2 \to 42.3$, $-3.9$; 10.2; 1.6; 5.6. RoboCasa365 (13 defect tasks only, App. E): GR00T N1.5 (100%) $41.2 \to 38.8$, $-2.4$; 5.8; 0.0; 2.4. GR00T N1.5 (30%) $37.7 \to 33.8$, $-3.8$; 12.2; 1.2; 5.4. Xiaomi-Robotics-1 $38.2 \to 34.8$, $-3.4$; 12.5; 2.2; 6.1. REKI-2B $29.8 \to 28.2$, $-1.5$; 5.1; 0.0; 1.5. RoboDojo (11 defect tasks, layouts 0-9, App. E): Rex-M1 $35.5 \to 40.0$, $+4.5$; 0.0; 7.0; 4.5. VPP $30.0 \to 39.1$, $+9.1$; 0.0; 13.0; 9.1. Awomo-0.5 $20.0 \to 21.0$, $+1.0$; 0.0; 1.2; 1.0. Xiaomi-Robotics-1 $10.9 \to 11.8$, $+0.9$; 0.0; 1.0; 0.9. StarVLA (QwenPI) $5.5 \to 9.1$, $+3.6$; 0.0; 3.8; 3.6. StarVLA (QwenOFT) $0.9 \to 5.5$, $+4.5$; 0.0; 4.6; 4.5. Absolute episode counts are not in the text; Table 4 (App. E) gives RoboTwin flip counts by repair type (press without contact 6 / 23 / 20 / 24 / 19; missing condition 0 / 2 / 4 / 3 / 9; command-based grasp 0 / 0 / 5 / 3 / 7; transient success 2 / 9 / 13 / 11 / 15; silent failures 0 / 1 / 13 / 7 / 9 for LingBot-VA / LingBot-VLA 2.0 / Evo-1 / X-VLA / $\pi_{0.5}$), so for $\pi_{0.5}$ 59 flips at 5.6% imply $N \approx 1{,}050$ episodes per policy on RoboTwin (inference from Tables 2 and 4). Table 1 (audit counts): defects RoboTwin 31 (25 tasks), RoboCasa365 18 (13), RoboDojo 12 (11); phantom 20 / 17 / 3, silent 11 / 1 / 9; by cause, missing condition 10 / 7 / 0 = 17, unstated requirement 5 / 1 / 9 = 15, proxy signal 15 / 0 / 1 = 16, loose geometry 0 / 8 / 2 = 10, transient success 1 / 2 / 0 = 3; 'The cause of a defect fixes its direction' except the proxy, 'with 10 phantom successes and 6 silent failures' (sec. 4.2).
load_bearing_assumption: That the instruction string is the specification and a person's reading of rendered frames is the ground truth: 'A person who reads the instruction and looks at the scene decides whether it is fulfilled' (sec. 3.1), so every condition a checker tests that the instruction does not mention is a defect ('the Verified checker removes every condition that the instruction does not mention', sec. 3.3). If the benchmark authors' intent, not the instruction string, is the specification, then the 15 unstated-requirement defects and most of RoboDojo's 9 silent failures (the digit 8 'rejected after a half turn that the instruction does not mention', sec. 4.2) are tolerance choices rather than errors, and RoboDojo's +0.9 to +9.1 pp (Table 2) is a redefinition of the task, not a correction. Second, that the Verified checker is itself right: it is a second hand-written checker whose validation is 1,233 expert episodes plus the 61 states that defined it (sec. 3.3); its force-based release test, one-second persistence and condition removals are never audited by the same pipeline. Third, that the staged states are states policies visit: tested only on the tasks where the audit found a defect for RoboCasa365 (13 tasks) and RoboDojo (11 tasks), and on all 50 tasks for RoboTwin 2.0 (App. E).
weakest_component: Recall and the two attrition steps. Precision is complete (two annotators 'confirm every defect', sec. 4.3) but recall is bounded only by the agent's cap of four hypotheses per task and by a 50-item sample of the roughly 122 rejected candidates ('found no valid defects among them', sec. 4.3); of 568 proposed states only 183 produced the predicted verdict, and the text does not split the other 385 between wrong code reading and probes that failed to build the state. Next: (1) the re-evaluation on RoboCasa365 and RoboDojo covers only the 13 and 11 tasks with a defect (App. E), so the RoboCasa365 and RoboDojo rows of Table 2 are success rates over defect tasks, not benchmark-level shifts, while RoboTwin's rows are over all 50 tasks; the three benchmarks' deltas are not on one scale; (2) no published leaderboard number is re-scored, every number is the authors' own re-rolls of released checkpoints 'under the benchmark’s official protocol' (sec. 4.4), and the number of episodes per policy is not stated; (3) the largest flip group in Table 4, 'pressing without touching' where 'the original checker accepts a contact point that the simulator reports across an air gap of up to 2 cm' (App. E), is a repair type that does not appear by that name in the five-cause taxonomy, and RoboTwin has zero loose-geometry defects in Table 1, so the audit's defect accounting and the rollout flip accounting do not reconcile one to one; (4) the LLM agent and VLM reviewer models are unnamed (not in text), and the reviewer's 'wrong' label ('the state the checker accepts is a reasonable success', sec. 3.2) is a judgement call that decides 19 of 91 RoboTwin candidates (App. D); (5) rankings 'stayed the same on all three benchmarks' (sec. 4.4), so the leaderboard consequence the paper motivates with is, on its own evidence, nil.
regime: Benchmarks: RoboTwin 2.0 (bimanual, 50 tasks in the clean setting, official seeds, expert filter, unseen instructions; App. E), RoboCasa365 and RoboDojo; 142 tasks audited in total (sec. 1), split across the latter two not in text. Audit scale: 568 candidate states, 183 agent-confirmed, 61 defects in 49 tasks (Table 1). Cost: $0.78 in LLM calls and 18 minutes per task on average including simulator probes (App. D). Models used by the pipeline (LLM agent, VLM reviewer): unknown (not in text). Policies re-scored (sec. 4.4; Table 2): RoboTwin 2.0 LingBot-VA, LingBot-VLA 2.0, Evo-1, X-VLA, $\pi_{0.5}$ (Motus checkpoint), original success 46.2-93.9%; RoboCasa365 GR00T N1.5 fine-tuned on 100% and 30% of training data, Xiaomi-Robotics-1, REKI-2B, 29.8-41.2% on 13 defect tasks, with $\pi_{0.5}$ and $\pi_{0}$ named as evaluated with no verdict changes but no Table 2 row; RoboDojo Rex-M1, VPP, Awomo-0.5, Xiaomi-Robotics-1, StarVLA QwenPI and QwenOFT, 0.9-35.5% on 11 defect tasks, layouts 0-9. Horizon: episode time limits not stated numerically; persistence window 1 s; a stack 'is falling' within 60 ms (App. C); physics step not stated. Policies are imitation-trained VLA and world-action models by their citations; no statement in the text that any was trained with the checker as reward. Episodes per policy: not stated (about 1,050 on RoboTwin by inference from Tables 2 and 4). Verified checker validated on 1,233 expert episodes (sec. 3.3). Human annotation: two annotators on all 61 defects and on 50 sampled rejections (sec. 4.3). Release: 'We release SimAudit, the repaired checkers, and the rendered counterexamples' (sec. 5); URL not in text. arXiv v1, 18 Nov 2026, cs.CV and cs.RO; venue not stated.
information_asymmetry: Three asymmetries, one per stage the paper's own pipeline separates. (1) Code vs executed state. From the checker code and the instruction alone, the Read stage can see the specification gap, which cause classes missing condition (17 of 61 defects) and unstated requirement (15 of 61) live in, and it can see that a proxy is read (commanded gripper value, 16 of 61) or that a region is permissive (loose geometry, 10 of 61); it cannot see whether a reachable physical state falls into the gap: 'A hypothesis is a claim about code until the state exists' (sec. 3.2). The attrition measures this: of 568 proposed states 183 returned the predicted verdict (sec. 1), and on RoboTwin 37 of 91 confirmed hypotheses were 'unrealistic' (teleport-only), 19 'wrong' and 3 'not shown' (App. D), so about two thirds of what the code predicts is not a defect on any reachable state. Two cause classes exist only in time-evolved physics and no code reading reveals them: transient success (3 of 61; a stack that passes at the first step and 'Within 60 ms, the stack is falling', App. C) and the first-step gripper phantom (the checker 'turns true on the first physics step after the open command, with the fingers still closed on the object', App. C). The largest rollout-flip source, pressing without contact, is a simulator-side quantity, 'a contact point that the simulator reports across an air gap of up to 2 cm' (App. E), a contact-reporting artifact the checker inherits and that only the executed rollout exposes. (2) Staged states vs visited states. The audit constructs states; whether policies reach them is a separate measurement, done by scoring the same rollouts twice (sec. 4.4). The paper did not re-score any published leaderboard number; it re-ran released checkpoints under the official protocol and reports percentages without episode counts (Table 2). Movement: RoboTwin 2.0, all 50 tasks, $\Delta$ of $-2.7$ to $-3.9$ pp, phantom share 3.3-10.2% of original successes, silent share 0.0-3.9% of original failures, flips 3.1-5.6% of episodes (about 1,050 per policy by inference from Table 4); RoboCasa365, 13 defect tasks only, $\Delta$ $-1.5$ to $-3.8$ pp, phantom share 5.1-12.5%, flips 1.5-6.1%; RoboDojo, 11 defect tasks only, $\Delta$ $+0.9$ to $+9.1$ pp, silent share 1.0-13.0%, flips 0.9-9.1%. 'the rankings stayed the same on all three benchmarks' (sec. 4.4). Per task the effect is large and policy-specific: on 'click bell' $\pi_{0.5}$ keeps none of its successes, 'LingBot-VA keeps all of its successes, and X-VLA falls from 95% to 20%' (sec. 4.4); 'The flips concentrate in 4 to 19 of the 50 tasks, and they are largely the same tasks for every policy' (App. E). (3) Exploitation vs omission. The paper's frame is reachability, not exploitation: it asks 'how often released policies reach them' (sec. 4.4); the words exploit and hack do not occur, and no policy is said to have been trained with the checker as reward. It states the identifiability problem exactly and leaves it: 'A policy that goes on to release is therefore credited early, and a policy that stops there is credited for a task it did not finish. The recorded episode is the same in both cases' (App. C); in all ten continued RoboTwin probes 'the object ended in the correct place'. The only evidence that policy behaviour interacts with a defect is the differential sensitivity across policies on one task (95% to 20% vs no loss). Checkers missing real successes are measured directly as the silent share (up to 13.0% of VPP's RoboDojo failures). Inference (not in text): the missing ruler is per step on the policy's visited states, the L5 shape with the checker in place of the solver: for each rollout, the time from the original checker's first success to physical completion (release force zero, contact, one-second persistence), and whether an RL-trained policy's visitation concentrates at accepted-but-unfinished states relative to an imitation-trained one on the same tasks; that comparison would separate a reward-hacked checker from an accident of early termination, and nothing in the paper runs it.
occupies: Published: the two-type vocabulary (phantom success, silent failure) and a five-cause taxonomy (missing condition, unstated requirement, proxy signal, loose geometry, transient success) for hand-written success checkers; an LLM-plus-simulator audit pipeline (instruction and code read separately, up to four staged counterexamples per task under physics, code-blind VLM review of multi-view renders) with 61 human-confirmed defects in 49 of 142 tasks across RoboTwin 2.0 (31), RoboCasa365 (18) and RoboDojo (12), with the direction per benchmark (RoboCasa365 over-credits, RoboDojo under-credits, RoboTwin both; Table 1); repaired 'Verified' checkers for the three benchmarks (physical-state measurement, instruction-matched conditions, one-second persistence) validated on 1,233 expert episodes; and a same-rollout re-scoring of 15 released policy checkpoints showing $-3.9$ to $+9.1$ pp shifts, up to 9.1% of a policy's episodes flipped, and unchanged rankings (Table 2); the released pipeline, checkers and rendered counterexamples (sec. 5). Not claimed in the text: re-scoring of published leaderboard numbers; benchmark-level shifts for RoboCasa365 and RoboDojo (defect tasks only); any statement that policies exploit checker defects or were trained against them; recall of the audit beyond a 50-item sample; the models used in the pipeline.

neighbors.title: Faster and Better? Benchmark Bugs and Design Limitations Distort the Evaluation of Vision-Language-Action Acceleration
neighbors.trick: Start from tasks where an approximation of a policy scores above the policy, plot object trajectories against checker acceptance regions, and find 22 bugs and 4 design limitations across seven benchmarks whose fixes reverse method rankings (abstract, fetched); cited here as 'The study most closely related to ours is a manual audit of LIBERO and its variants, as well as RoboTwin, RoboCasa, and VLABench' (sec. 2), and this paper differs by automating the search over every task, documenting each defect with a reproducible state and render, and counting verdict changes on released policies.

neighbors.title: When the Simulator Fails, Not the Policy: Auditing Contact Artifacts in Simulated Robot Benchmarks

theme_fit.why: same instrument shape as the lane's per-step audit, a reference observer run beside the released scorer on the states policies actually visit (the Verified checker 'reads the simulator state at every step at which the original checker is evaluated and never changes it', sec. 3.3), applied to the success checker instead of the solver; the largest flip source is a contact-reporting artifact (a contact point 'across an air gap of up to 2 cm', App. E) that sits on the lane's simulator-fidelity side; the lane's exploit question (does a policy trained against the artifact concentrate on it) is stated as an identifiability problem (App. C) and not measured

a benchmark-validity audit of the judge (outcome validity in the paper's own citation of the Agentic Benchmark Checklist, sec. 2) with a differential re-scoring that attributes verdict changes to named checker repairs per policy (Table 4); the object is a manipulation policy benchmark, not an agent loop, and the paper re-scores its own re-rolls rather than published numbers, so for the lane it is a method and a neighbour, not an answer
the same words (a checker is a sparse reward; phantom success is a reward-hacking surface) but a different problem; no training is run and no policy is said to have been trained against the checker

limitations_as_complaints: My benchmark ends the episode at the first success verdict, so when the repaired checker says the object was still in the gripper I cannot tell a policy that would have released from one that had stopped, and the paper that found the defect cannot either: 'A policy that goes on to release is therefore credited early, and a policy that stops there is credited for a task it did not finish. The recorded episode is the same in both cases.' (App. C); 'Both are judged on the state at which the benchmark gives its verdict; what the robot would have done after the episode ends does not count.' (sec. 3.1).

I want to know how much the number on the leaderboard moves when the checker is fixed, and the re-scoring gives me that for RoboTwin 2.0 only; on the other two benchmarks it scores the defect tasks alone, never the published numbers, and the rankings did not change: 'On RoboCasa365 we evaluate 13 tasks in which the audit found a defect.' and 'evaluate 11 tasks in which the audit found a defect, on layouts 0 to 9 of each task.' (App. E); 'the rankings stayed the same on all three benchmarks, even as rescoring changed how closely some policies matched their nearest competitors.' (sec. 4.4).

The audit tells me the 61 defects it found are real, but not how many it missed: four hypotheses per task, two thirds of confirmed candidates thrown out by a VLM reviewer, and the recall check is a sample of fifty, with a human reading of the instruction as the only ground truth: 'Of the 183 candidates for which the checker returned the predicted verdict, approximately two-thirds were rejected during visual review.' and 'The annotators then examined a random sample of 50 rejected candidates and found no valid defects among them.' (sec. 4.3); 'A person who reads the instruction and looks at the scene decides whether it is fulfilled.' (sec. 3.1).
